extraction.name: Natural Questions
extraction.description: Natural Questions (NQ) is a question answering data set consisting of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine. Each question is paired with a Wikipedia page from the top 5 search results, and annotators mark a long answer (typically a paragraph or table) and a short answer (one or more entities) if present on the page, or mark null if no answer is present. The public release consists of 307,373 training examples with single annotations; 7,830 examples with 5-way annotations for development data; and 7,842 examples with 5-way annotations sequestered as test data.
extraction.creator: Google Research
extraction.citeAs: Kwiatkowski, T., Palomaki, J., Redfield, O., Collins, M., Parikh, A., Alberti, C., Epstein, D., Polosukhin, I., Devlin, J., Lee, K., Toutanova, K., Jones, L., Kelcey, M., Chang, M.-W., Dai, A. M., Uszkoreit, J., Le, Q., & Petrov, S. (2019). Natural Questions: A Benchmark for Question Answering Research. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 7, 453-466.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions consist of real anonymized, aggregated queries of 8 words or more issued to the Google search engine by multiple users in a short period of time. A subset is sampled using heuristics targeting likely questions (e.g., starting with 'who', 'when', 'where', containing categorical noun phrases). Questions are run through the Google search engine and retained if a Wikipedia page appears in the top 5 search results. The resulting (question, Wikipedia page) pairs are then presented to human annotators who provide long and short answer annotations.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Passive Data Collection, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: 51% of examples have no long answer labeled; the authors consider the choice of whether or not to answer as a core part of the task and do not discard these examples. Annotators mark null when no viable answer candidates exist on the Wikipedia page.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine, paired with Wikipedia pages appearing in the top 5 search results for those queries.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Queries were filtered using heuristics: only queries of 8 or more words were considered; queries must match one of five syntactic patterns (starting with 'who'/'when'/'where' followed by specific verbs, containing multiple entities with modifiers, or containing/ending with categorical noun phrases). Queries without a Wikipedia page in the top 5 Google search results were discarded. Part of speech tags and entities were identified using Google's Cloud NLP API, and categorical noun phrases were pre-defined by running Hearst patterns.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotation follows a three-stage process completed by a single annotator per example: (1) Question Identification - determine if the question is good (fact-seeking) or bad (ambiguous, opinion-seeking, etc.) based solely on question content; (2) Long Answer Identification - for good questions, select the earliest HTML bounding box (paragraph, table, list item, or whole list) containing enough information to infer the answer, or mark 'no answer'; (3) Short Answer Identification - for examples with long answers, select the entity or set of entities answering the question, flag yes/no, or flag no short answer possible. Comprehensive guidelines were developed and annotation quality was constantly monitored.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: A custom annotation interface developed for the task.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Post hoc evaluation by four experts classified answers into Correct (C), Correct but debatable (Cd), or Wrong (W), with a consensus judgment for each example. Long answer precision is 90% and short answer precision is 84%. 25-way annotations on 302 examples were used to study annotator variability, showing that the proportion of annotators giving non-null answers correlates strongly with annotation correctness. The most popular long answer accounts for 83% of long answer annotations; the most popular short answer accounts for 64% of short answer annotations.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Training set: 1 annotation per item (307,373 examples). Development set: 5 annotations per item (7,830 examples). Test set: 5 annotations per item (7,842 examples). A subset of 302 examples has 25-way annotations.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: A pool of around 50 annotators with an average annotation time of 80 seconds per example. No further demographic details are provided.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Google's Cloud NLP API was used for identifying part of speech tags and entities during question filtering (not for answer annotation itself).
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Questions consist of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine. Queries were anonymized and aggregated (multiple users in a short period) before use.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset focuses on longer queries (8+ words) and excludes 'how to' questions, potentially biasing the question distribution toward more complex factual questions. The focus on Wikipedia as the source of evidence documents may introduce biases, though the authors believe Wikipedia is stylistically similar to other factual web sources. There is genuine ambiguity and variability in acceptable answers for naturally occurring questions.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The data set currently focuses on longer queries, excludes 'how to' questions, and uses only Wikipedia as the evidence source. Future data collection efforts may introduce shorter queries, 'how to' questions, or other domains. For naturally occurring questions there is often genuine ambiguity and multiple acceptable answers. Baseline models lag significantly behind the super-annotator upper bound, indicating the task is far from solved. Boolean (yes/no) answers are left to future work in baselines.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Intended as a benchmark for question answering research, providing large-scale end-to-end training data for QA and driving research in natural language understanding. Use cases include Training (307,373 single-annotation examples), Validation/Development (7,830 5-way annotated examples), and Testing (7,842 5-way annotated examples, sequestered). Evaluation uses precision, recall, and F1 metrics robust to annotation variability.
